99.title: Covering the eyes
99.hook: hands circle the candle flames, then cover the eyes while the blessing is said
99.howItsDone: Shabbat candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday; the person lighting often circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes, says the blessing, and many add quiet words of their own before uncovering their eyes to look at the light.

segments.voice: Yesterday, erev Shabbat, and your line: get ready for a guest. Now the guest arrives.

Most people have a place to get ten seconds alone. The car in the driveway, engine off. The stairwell at work. You put your face in your hands, and for a moment nobody needs anything from you. In many Jewish homes, those ten seconds come at the same time every week. Friday, just before sunset, the candles are lit. The hands circle the flames, then come up over the eyes, and the person lighting stands in the dark of their own palms while the blessing is said. Often they stay there a little longer than the blessing takes.
screen: `TEN SECONDS ALONE.` → `HANDS CIRCLE THE FLAMES.` → `A LITTLE LONGER THAN THE BLESSING.`

segments.voice: On day two you met the two flames, and the reason for the hands: once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, so people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look. Today, stay behind the hands a little longer. The blessing is short: it thanks God, who commanded the lighting of the Sabbath lamp. But in many homes the hands don't come down right away. People speak quietly, in their own words. For centuries this was one of the few moments in the week that belonged to the woman of the house, and people wrote prayers for it. From the sixteen hundreds on, Jewish women in central and eastern Europe used small books of personal prayers in Yiddish, called tkhines. Many include one for the candles: for a husband's livelihood, for a sick parent, for children who would grow up to love learning. Not the language of the official prayer book: the language of the kitchen. And the rabbis took their model of personal prayer from a woman. In the first book of Samuel, Hannah, longing for a child, prays at the sanctuary in Shiloh. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The priest Eli decides she's drunk. The Talmud reads the scene the other way: this is how to pray. The heart turned toward the words, the lips moving, the voice kept low. Watch someone at the candles and you'll often see exactly that. Then the hands come down, and the week is over.
screen: `ON DAY TWO: LIGHT, COVER, BLESS.` · `THE HANDS STAY UP A LITTLE LONGER.` · `TKHINES: PRAYERS IN THE KITCHEN'S LANGUAGE.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · then, large: `ONLY HER LIPS MOVED.`

segments.voice: Light a candle if it's safe, or just picture one, and rest your hands over your eyes for three slow breaths. On the first, let the week's noise go quiet; on the second, think of someone you'd hold in your heart if you pray, or simply wish well if you don't. On the third, lower your hands and look at the first thing you see as if it were new.
Tkhines, small books of personal prayers in Yiddish that Jewish women wrote, for the candles and more.
Your line: eyes closed, the week ends. Behind the hands it ends, and then you look up at the light. Day ninety-nine, done.

100.title: Shalom Aleichem
100.hook: the Friday night song welcomes angels; the Talmud says two walk you home (Shabbat 119b)
100.tomorrow: a guest at the Friday table
100.howItsDone: On Friday night, after returning from synagogue and before Kiddush, many families stand around the table and sing Shalom Aleichem, each of its four verses three times.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tkhines, the women's prayers said at the candles: light, cover, bless, then look. Your line was eyes closed, the week ends. And this is day one hundred. A hundred days. That's worth a breath on its own.

Friday night, the walk home from synagogue. The streets are quieter than usual. Somebody has a child on their shoulders. Maybe it's cold, maybe it's warm and you can hear other families' dinners through open windows. You open your door: the candles are already burning, the table is set. And before anyone sits down, the family stands around the table and starts to sing. Not to each other. To guests nobody can see.
screen: `THE WALK HOME ON FRIDAY NIGHT.` → `THE CANDLES ARE BURNING.` → `A SONG FOR GUESTS NO ONE CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Shalom aleichem means peace be upon you. It's also an everyday greeting, a hello in Hebrew and Yiddish. But on Friday night it's a song, sung to angels. The idea comes from a story in the Talmud. Two ministering angels, it says, walk a person home from synagogue on Friday night, one good and one bad. If the candles are lit, the table is set and the beds are made, the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat too. And the bad angel has no choice but to answer amen. If the house is dark and nothing's ready, it goes the other way around, and the good angel has to say amen. It's a story about habit: the way you welcome this week shapes the next. The song is much younger than the story. Tradition traces it to Kabbalist circles, many centuries after the Talmud. It has four short verses, often each sung three times. Welcome, angels of peace. Come in peace. Bless me with peace. Go in peace. Some people ask, reasonably, why you'd tell angels to leave. One answer is simple courtesy: they walked you home, and now you can let them go. Another is that the family is about to sit down together, and some moments are just for the people at the table. Families sing it to many tunes, fast and slow. Some hold hands. Some sing it once, quietly, alone. It turns an ordinary doorway into the place where the week's peace comes in.

segments.voice: Picture the next door you'll walk through, home, work, a friend's place, and your hand on it. Pick any tune that feels like peace to you and hum a little of it, even under your breath. Picture walking through that door humming, with two quiet companions beside you, noticing what kind of place you've made.
Shalom Aleichem. Peace be upon you: a greeting, and the Friday night song that welcomes the angels of peace home.
Your line: angels walk you home. Come in peace, go in peace. That's day one hundred.

101.title: A guest at the Friday table
101.hook: invited to a Friday-night dinner for the first time: what happens, and what nobody expects of you
101.carry: you don't have to know the words
101.howItsDone: Many Jewish families and communities invite guests for Friday-night dinner, including friends, partners and people who would otherwise be alone; guests are welcome to follow along, ask questions and join in as much or as little as they like.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shalom Aleichem: the song for the two angels who walk you home. Your line was angels walk you home. Today, someone else is walking through the door: a guest.

The text says: come for Shabbat dinner, Friday, seven. Maybe it's your partner's parents. Maybe a coworker, a college Hillel, a friend who just started hosting. Maybe you're Jewish and have never actually been to one. And the questions start. What do I bring? Do I need to know Hebrew? What if everyone stands up and I'm still sitting? A Friday table is built for guests. Inviting people, especially people with nowhere else to go, is one of the oldest parts of Shabbat. Today: what to expect when you're the one walking in.
screen: `COME FOR SHABBAT DINNER.` → `DO I NEED HEBREW?` → `A TABLE BUILT FOR GUESTS.`

segments.voice: Start at the door. The greeting is Shabbat shalom, a peaceful Sabbath. In some homes you'll hear the Yiddish, gut Shabbos. Either is perfect. Come on time, or a little early, because in many homes the candles are lit before sunset, and in observant homes the host won't drive, cook, or answer the phone once Shabbat begins. Flowers are a safe gift. If you'd like to bring food or wine, ask first, since many hosts keep kosher. Then the evening has an order, and most of it is joyful. A song, often Shalom Aleichem. In many homes, parents bless their children. Then Kiddush, the blessing over a cup of wine or grape juice; some families stand for it, some sit, and you just do what the table does. Then the part that surprises guests. Many people get up and wash their hands at a sink, pouring water from a cup, and then go quiet. Nobody's upset. There's a custom of not talking between washing and the blessing over the bread, so the two stay joined. Then the challah is blessed, often sprinkled with salt, torn and passed around. And then dinner, which can go on for hours. What nobody expects of you: to know the Hebrew, to sing along, or to pretend to be anything you're not. Listening is enough. Asking is better. What's this for? is a question most hosts are delighted to answer. The rabbis even taught that welcoming guests is greater than receiving the Divine Presence. You're not intruding on the evening. You're part of what it's for.
screen: `SHABBAT SHALOM AT THE DOOR.` · `CANDLES, SONG, BLESSINGS, WINE.` · `WASH, THEN A QUIET MOMENT.` · `NOBODY EXPECTS THE WORDS.`

102.title: Kiddush
102.hook: a cup of wine or grape juice declares the day holy, remembering creation and the Exodus
102.howItsDone: On Friday night, before the meal, someone at the table lifts a cup of wine or grape juice and recites Kiddush, beginning with Genesis 2:1–3, and everyone then takes a sip.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a guest at the Friday table: Shabbat shalom at the door, and a quiet moment after washing. Your line was you don't have to know the words. Today, the cup a guest sees lifted first.
screen: `YOU DON'T HAVE TO KNOW THE WORDS.`

segments.voice: At a wedding, someone taps a glass, everyone stands, and a toast turns an ordinary evening into an occasion. Same room, same people. But now it's official: this night matters. On Friday night, in Jewish homes, there's a moment like that at the table. Someone lifts a full cup of wine or grape juice, the room goes quiet, and the words turn a Friday evening into something else.
screen: `SOMEONE TAPS A GLASS.` → `NOW IT'S OFFICIAL.` → `A FULL CUP ON FRIDAY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Kiddush means making holy, from the same root as kadosh, holy. It comes from the commandment, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." The rabbis asked: how do you remember a day? You say so, out loud, over a cup of wine, the drink of celebration. Grape juice works too, and some families use it. If there's no wine at all, the blessing can be said over the challah. On Friday night, Kiddush begins with the last lines of the creation story in Genesis: "And the heaven and the earth were finished, and all the host of them." Then God rested on the seventh day and blessed it. Next comes the blessing over the fruit of the vine, then a longer blessing that names two reasons for the day. Shabbat is a remembrance of creation, the world God made and finished. And it's a reminder of the Exodus, leaving Egypt. Why the Exodus? In Deuteronomy, the Sabbath commandment says: remember that you were a slave in Egypt. Slaves don't get days off. Free people do. So every Friday night, one cup holds two memories: the world was made, and the slaves went free. Customs vary. Some stand, some sit. Some hold the cup in the palm of the hand. Afterward, everyone takes a sip, often from little cups poured from the big one. It's short. But like the toast at a wedding, it says out loud: this time is different.
screen: `KIDDUSH: MAKING HOLY.` · `REMEMBER IT OVER WINE.` · `CREATION, AND LEAVING EGYPT.` · `FREE PEOPLE REST.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE SABBATH DAY, TO KEEP IT HOLY.`

segments.voice: Pick up whatever drink is near you, water or coffee is fine, or picture one. Think of one thing in your life you didn't make but get to enjoy, and one way you're more free than you once were. Lift the cup a little and say one sentence of thanks, out loud if you can, to God if you pray, then drink slowly.
Kiddush. Making holy: a blessing over wine or grape juice that declares Shabbat holy, remembering creation and the Exodus.

103.title: Two loaves
103.hook: two loaves recall the double manna; they stay covered while the wine is blessed
103.howItsDone: At Shabbat meals, two loaves of challah sit covered on the table during Kiddush; then the cover is removed, the blessing over bread is said, and the challah is often salted, torn and shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kiddush: one cup for two memories, creation and freedom. Your line was make it holy out loud.

Friday morning, a bakery in a Jewish neighborhood. The loaves are stacked up: shiny, golden, braided, soft inside, a little sweet. Customer after customer asks for two, and by noon the shelves are nearly bare. On the Friday night table there's another odd detail: the loaves sit under a cloth, often embroidered, sometimes made by a child at school, while the wine is blessed. Two loaves, under a cloth, waiting their turn.
screen: `A FRIDAY MORNING BAKERY.` → `ASK FOR TWO.` → `COVERED, WAITING THEIR TURN.`

segments.voice: Why two? Go back to the manna, a few days ago on this path. Every morning in the wilderness, bread from heaven, enough for one day. But on the sixth day, the Torah says, the people gathered twice as much, a double portion, because nothing would fall on Shabbat. So the Shabbat table has two loaves, lechem mishneh, double bread, to remember the double manna. Two loaves say: there was enough, even for the day nobody gathered. Now the name. In the Torah, challah is actually the portion of dough set aside for the priests. Some bakers still pinch off a small piece of dough and set it aside before baking, with a blessing, and the whole loaf came to be called by that name. The braids are a custom, not a law. They're common among Ashkenazi Jews, whose families came from central and eastern Europe; other communities bake flat breads or round loaves, and round loaves are a New Year custom. Why the cloth? There are several answers. One says the manna lay between two layers of dew, one below and one above, so the bread sits on a board and under a cover. Another is so gentle it's told as a children's story too: normally bread's blessing comes first, so the bread is covered so it won't be embarrassed while the wine goes ahead of it. The lesson people draw: if even a loaf's feelings count, so does everyone's at the table. Then the cover comes off, the blessing is said, and the bread, often sprinkled with salt, is torn and passed around.
screen: `TWO LOAVES FOR THE DOUBLE MANNA.` · `CHALLAH: THE PORTION SET ASIDE.` · `BRAIDED, ROUND OR FLAT.` · `COVERED, LIKE DEW OVER MANNA.` · then, large: `THERE WAS ENOUGH.`

104.title: A woman of valor (Proverbs 31:10–31)
104.hook: many homes sing Eshet Chayil on Friday night to honor the women of the house
104.howItsDone: In many homes, Eshet Chayil (Proverbs 31:10–31) is sung at the Friday night table before Kiddush, often by a husband to his wife or by the whole family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, challah: two loaves for the double manna, covered while the wine is blessed. Your line was two loaves, enough.

Somebody in your life keeps everything running and almost never hears about it. They know where the birth certificates are, remember everyone's allergies, and fix the thing before anyone notices it's broken. When did someone last say, out loud, in front of everybody, what they do? In many Jewish homes on Friday night, someone at the table does exactly that, in a song whose words come straight from the Bible.
screen: `THE ONE WHO KEEPS IT RUNNING.` → `SAID OUT LOUD, IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.` → `A SONG FROM THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: It's the last chapter of the book of Proverbs, and it opens, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "A woman of valour who can find? For her price is far above rubies." Eshet is woman. Chayil is a strong word: strength, ability, even an army. Valor is a good translation. This isn't a delicate portrait. The woman in the poem buys a field, plants a vineyard, runs a business, stays up late, gets up before dawn, feeds her household, opens her hand to the poor, and speaks with wisdom and kindness. "Strength and dignity are her clothing," it says. The poem is an acrostic: its twenty-two verses begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, alef to tav, as if to say, praise her with every letter there is. In many homes it's sung on Friday night, often by a husband to his wife, sometimes by the whole family. The Kabbalists who made it part of the Friday night table also read it about Shabbat itself, or about God's presence, the Shekhinah, and some read it about the Torah. Jews read it in different ways today. Some sing it to wives and mothers, some to every woman at the table. Some feel its ideal is a heavy one to live up to, and choose other readings, or sing it to honor someone they've lost. The book of Ruth calls Ruth a woman of valor too, with the same Hebrew words. And the poem ends with public praise: "let her works praise her in the gates." Don't keep it private. Say it where people can hear.

105.title: What isn't done, and why (Mishnah Shabbat 7:2)
105.hook: thirty-nine kinds of creative work, linked to building the tabernacle, are set aside
105.howItsDone: Observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of melacha from sundown Friday until Saturday night, preparing food, lights and other needs in advance; other Jews keep some of them or set aside work in their own ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eshet chayil, praise sung out loud on Friday night. Your line was say the praise. That ends a week at the Friday table: candles, the angels' song, the children's blessing, Kiddush, challah and Eshet Chayil.

You can carry a heavy table across the living room, and on Shabbat it's fine. But in many observant homes, you won't flip a light switch, or write a two-letter word on a sticky note. That sounds backward. Moving furniture is hard; writing is easy. If Shabbat is about rest, why is the easy thing off the table? Because the Hebrew word usually translated as work doesn't mean effort at all.
screen: `CARRY A TABLE: FINE.` → `WRITE TWO LETTERS: NOT TODAY.` → `WORK ISN'T EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Melacha means creative work: the kind that makes something, changes the world, or puts your stamp on it. The Torah says don't do melacha on Shabbat, but it barely says what melacha is. One example it does give, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." So how did the rabbis define it? Right after that verse, the Torah turns to building the mishkan, the tabernacle that closed camp two. Shabbat and the mishkan, side by side. So the rabbis said: whatever kinds of work it took to build the mishkan, those are the kinds you set aside on Shabbat. Six days a week, you can build a holy place in space. On the seventh, you stop, and live in holy time. The Mishnah lists them: forty less one, thirty-nine. They read like a tour of a workshop in the ancient world. Sowing, plowing, reaping, grinding, kneading, baking. Shearing, dyeing, spinning, weaving, sewing. Writing two letters, erasing. Building, tearing down. Kindling a fire, putting one out. Carrying from one domain to another. Later rabbis' rulings about modern life, from cars to electricity, grow out of those thirty-nine, and Jewish movements apply them differently. Orthodox Jews keep them in detail. Other Jews keep some, or choose their own ways to rest. The idea underneath is the same, and it's a surprising one: for one day, you stop being the one who shapes the world, and let the world be.
